"Tea, Phuppo?"
"Less sugar. Your grandfather gave everything to the boys, you know. The house, the shop. Me? A suitcase and a husband."
"I know, Phuppo. You've told me."
"I could have sung on the radio. Did anyone ask? No."
Rehana sat down beside her. "What would you have sung first?"
Zainab blinked. "Nobody asks that." She hummed two lines, then stopped. "Your mother thinks I'm bitter."
"I think you were wronged, and it still hurts."
"Hmph. And you, with your office job, don't end up like me."
Rehana squeezed her hand and said nothing clever. Later, washing the cups, she typed into her phone notes: Say the hard thing when it's happening. Don't store it for forty years.

qa.q: What did Zainab say she was given instead of the house and shop?
qa.a: A suitcase and a husband.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling, judging by the note she typed later?
qa.a: She felt compassion for Phuppo's hurt and a firm resolve not to store up her own grievances for forty years.

qa.q: Why did asking "What would you have sung first?" work better than arguing?
qa.a: It showed real interest in Zainab's lost dream instead of lecturing, so she softened and even hummed.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab when Rehana says she was wronged?
qa.a: She likely feels heard for once instead of dismissed as bitter, even if she answers gruffly.

grounding: A young woman listens to her aunt's old grievances with compassion and without lecturing, and resolves not to rehearse resentments herself.

passage: Every Eid I, Reena, sit next to Yusuf Nana, my mother's uncle, because nobody else will and Ammi says her daughter has the patience of a stone. By the second plate of biryani he is on the same list: the partner who cheated him out of the printing press in 1979, the brother who never repaid a loan, the novel he never finished because "people like us don't get published." This year I noticed my jaw tightening, ready to say, "Nana, let it go." I didn't. I asked what the novel was about. He talked for twenty minutes, his eyes brighter than I'd ever seen them. On the drive home I felt two things at once: sad for all the years he had spent rehearsing that list, and very clear about my own. I have a half-written grudge against my old manager. I'm not going to polish it for forty years.

qa.q: What did Yusuf Nana say about why he never finished his novel?
qa.a: That people like us don't get published.

qa.q: What two feelings did Reena have on the drive home?
qa.a: Sadness for the years Nana spent rehearsing his list, and a clear resolve not to keep polishing her own grudge.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make when her jaw tightened, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of saying "let it go", she asked what the novel was about, which let Nana speak about his dream instead of defending his grievances.

qa.q: Why might nobody else sit next to Yusuf Nana?
qa.a: Others may find the repeated complaints tiring and avoid them, which probably leaves him lonelier and more bitter.

grounding: A young woman sees an older relative stuck in old grievances, listens without lecturing and resolves not to rehearse her own resentments.

passage:
Day-centre volunteer log, Thursday. Hrithik, coordinator.
Mr Pankaj Joshi, 78, spent most of the carrom hour telling me again how juniors at the railway office were promoted over him and how his son "never calls." He pushed his tea away twice. I noticed he talks faster when he reaches 1992, the year of the transfer, and his hands tighten on the table. I didn't correct him or tell him to think positive. I asked what work he was proudest of. He described a timetable he had redesigned, in great detail, and smiled once.
Personal note: I recognise the edge in my own voice when I talk about my last boss. I don't want to be retelling it at 78.
Next: I'll ask Mr Joshi if he'd help the Saturday group plan the train-trip outing.

qa.q: What did Mr Joshi describe when asked about his proudest work?
qa.a: A timetable he had redesigned, in great detail.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's personal note reveal about Hrithik's feelings?
qa.a: Hrithik feels compassion for Mr Joshi and a resolve not to end up retelling an old grievance about a boss at 78.

qa.q: Why is inviting Mr Joshi to help plan the train trip a good next step?
qa.a: It uses the skill he is proud of and gives him something current to care about, instead of lecturing him to let go.

qa.q: How might Mr Joshi feel being asked about his proudest work rather than corrected?
qa.a: He may feel respected and seen for his skill, as his smile suggests, rather than dismissed as a complainer.

grounding: A young coordinator notices an older man dwelling on old grievances, listens without lecturing and resolves not to rehearse resentments himself.

passage:
Tuesday, late
Spent the afternoon with Dhruv Mama. Every visit it's the same story: the state exam in 1979, the paper that leaked, the cousin who got the post he says was his. Forty-five years, and he still tells it with his fists clenched. Today he added the brother-in-law who never repaid him and the son who "forgot" him.
I didn't correct him or tell him to let go. I just asked what he had wanted to do with that job. He went quiet, then said he'd wanted to build bridges in the hills. For five minutes he wasn't angry, only sad.
On the bus home I felt heavy for him. And I noticed my own jaw was tight about Deshpande taking credit for my report last month. I've told that story four times already.
I don't want to be seventy and still telling the Deshpande story. Stopping at four.
Yogesh

qa.q: What did Dhruv Mama say he had wanted to build?
qa.a: He had wanted to build bridges in the hills.

qa.q: What did Yogesh feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Yogesh felt heavy with compassion for Mama, and uneasy on noticing the grudge about Deshpande.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do instead of lecturing Dhruv Mama, and what came of it?
qa.a: Yogesh asked what Mama had wanted to do with the job, and for five minutes the anger turned into sadness that could be shared.

qa.q: What might it be like for Dhruv Mama to be asked about his hopes instead of being told to let go?
qa.a: He may feel heard for once, which let him show the sadness underneath the anger.

grounding: A young adult listens to an uncle rehearse old grievances without lecturing, feels compassion, and resolves not to end up rehearsing their own.

Simran: back from Bua's. drained
Rekha: the same stories?
Simran: the same. the dowry fight from 1985, the house Chacha got, how nobody thanked her for raising all of us cousins
Simran: she's right about some of it. that's the sad part
Rekha: did you argue?
Simran: no. I used to. today I just held her hand and let her talk. after an hour she calmed down and showed me her old embroidery
Rekha: that's kind
Simran: I kept thinking, she was 25 like me once. somewhere along the way the grudges became her whole house
Simran: I don't want that. I've been nursing the thing with my manager for a year
Rekha: so drop it?
Simran: not drop. just stop replaying it every night. and go back to Bua's next Sunday
Rekha: I'll come with you

qa.q: What did Bua show Simran after calming down?
qa.a: Her old embroidery.

qa.q: Why does Simran say 'she's right about some of it. that's the sad part'?
qa.a: Simran feels compassion because some of Bua's grievances are true, yet they have taken over Bua's whole life.

qa.q: What does Simran decide about the grudge with the manager?
qa.a: Not to drop it entirely but to stop replaying it every night, so it doesn't grow into a whole house of grudges.

qa.q: How might Bua have experienced Simran holding her hand instead of arguing?
qa.a: She may have felt listened to rather than judged, which is why she calmed down and brought out her embroidery.

grounding: A young adult listens without lecturing to an aunt who dwells on old grievances, feels compassion, and resolves not to rehearse a grudge of their own.
